argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Reconstructive interpretation followed by internal critique and resolution
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: Moderate - premises are often embedded in interpretive claims and logical analysis

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: High - engages with opposing views (Matthews) and anticipates objections
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: High - all sections directly support the thesis about Nietzsche's interpretive practice
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Moderate - relies on specific readings of Nietzsche and Heraclitus that may be contested

distinctions_drawn: Explanatory value vs. openness to experience

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Systematic - considers and rejects alternative solutions (preferred interpretation, will to power) before offering own
objections_raised: If no true world, how can interpretations be incorrect?
If no preferred perspective, how can one interpretation be better?
Will to power as criterion fails because Heraclitus's theory already exhibits it

appeals_to_authority: Nietzsche's texts (Ecce Homo, Twilight, Daybreak, Beyond Good and Evil, etc.)
named_thought_experiments: Karl Ernst's thought experiment on perception rate

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Continental philosophy (Nietzsche studies) with analytic rigor
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Interpretation, truth, perspectivism, will to power

summary_of_core_decisions: The essay reconstructs Nietzsche's interpretation of Heraclitus into three criteria (NC) and a fuller interpretation (NHI), then identifies paradoxes arising from Nietzsche's agreement/disagreement with those criteria. It resolves the paradoxes by proposing that acceptable interpretations must be open to new experiences and not claim absolute truth, thereby showing that Nietzsche does engage philosophically with the Presocratics.

thesis_commitment.conclusion_type: Interpretive thesis about Nietzsche's philosophical practice
